people.label: Zach King
people.intro: Zach King was born on February 4, 1990, in Portland, Oregon. This countdown ticks down to the next birthday of the digital magician famous for his seamless 'magic' video edits.
people.about: King got his start on Vine and YouTube with perfectly timed sleight-of-hand edits, and became one of the most-viewed creators on TikTok. His family-friendly illusions rack up billions of views, and he has written a children's book series on video magic.
facts: Born February 4, 1990, in Portland, Oregon
Launched FinalCutKing.com in 2008 to teach video editing after film school turned him down
His 2011 'Jedi Kittens' video hit a million views in three days
Named one of YouTube's 25 most promising young filmmakers in 2013
Holds the Guinness World Record for the most viewed TikTok video - his 2019 flying-broomstick illusion, with about 2.2 billion views
Author of the 'My Magical Life' children's book trilogy

timeline.text: Born February 4 in Portland, Oregon.
Launches FinalCutKing.com to teach video editing after film school turned him down.
Earns a Cinema and Media Arts degree from Biola University.
Joins Vine, posting a new "magic vine" every day for 30 days and becoming one of its biggest breakout stars.
Marries actress Rachel Holm.
Disney produces a Zootopia promo video inspired by one of his illusion clips.
Lands a 3-book deal with HarperCollins; Amblin Entertainment options film rights to his debut novel.
Posts "Zach King's Magic Broomstick," the video that becomes his record-holding TikTok.
Guinness World Records certifies the broomstick video as the most-viewed TikTok video ever.

sections.h: Rejected from film school, accepted by the internet
sections.p: King made his first movie at seven and applied to Biola University's film program as a teenager - and was rejected. So in 2008 he built FinalCutKing.com, teaching everyone Final Cut Pro and selling training seminars to pay tuition. In 2011 his 'Jedi Kittens' video - two cats duelling with lightsabers - hit a million views in three days. YouTube named him one of America's 25 most promising young filmmakers in 2013; that fall he moved to Vine, posting one impossible six-second trick a day.

sections.h: The broomstick that flew past two billion
sections.p: In December 2019, King glided down a suburban street on a flying broomstick in full Hogwarts uniform, captioned 'They rejected my application to Hogwarts but I still found a way to be a wizard.' The secret: a skateboard hidden behind a mirror, filmed in one afternoon with two friends. The clip became the most viewed video in TikTok history - a Guinness World Record verified at about 2.2 billion views - the perfect punchline for a kid once told no by film school.

sections.h: Magic that gives back
sections.p: King keeps his illusions strictly family-friendly, and he points that giant audience at good causes. He once pledged a penny to charity: water for every like on a TikTok over 24 hours, turning idle taps into clean-water funding, and in December 2024 he joined St. Jude Children's Research Hospital's GivingTuesday campaign, handing his channels over to spotlight St. Jude families. His book trilogy for kids carries the same message his career does: a 'no' is just the setup for the trick.

give.text: Give clean water through charity: water — the cause Zach funded penny by penny, one TikTok like at a time.

people.label: Dude Perfect
people.intro: Dude Perfect uploaded their very first video on April 9, 2009. Founded by five Texas roommates, the trick-shot crew became one of the most-subscribed channels on YouTube. This countdown runs to the anniversary of where it all began.
people.about: Coby Cotton, Cory Cotton, Garrett Hilbert, Cody Jones and Tyler Toney started filming backyard trick shots as Texas A&M roommates and turned it into a global sports-entertainment brand, with stadium tours, an app, and an 'Overtime' series watched by tens of millions.
facts: First video, 'Backyard Edition,' uploaded April 9, 2009
Founded by five Texas A&M roommates: Tyler Toney, Cody Jones, Garrett Hilbert, and twins Coby and Cory Cotton
Their first video hit 200,000 views in a week and was mentioned on Good Morning America
Set a Guinness World Record in 2016 with a 533-foot basketball shot from an Oklahoma City skyscraper

Kicks off its first-ever live arena tour.

sections.h: Five roommates, one backyard, 200,000 views
sections.p: Tyler Toney, Cody Jones, Garrett Hilbert, and twins Coby and Cory Cotton were Texas A&M roommates goofing around in Tyler's backyard when they filmed 'Backyard Edition' in April 2009 - a string of ridiculous basketball trick shots. Within a week it had 200,000 views and a mention on Good Morning America. The formula never changed: real shots, real celebrations, no fakery - just five friends who kept raising the hoop until the whole world was watching.

sections.h: 533 feet of nothing but net
sections.p: In 2016 the guys dropped a basketball shot from the top of the 533-foot Cotter Ranch Tower in Oklahoma City - a Guinness World Record for the greatest height from which a basketball has been shot. In a single record-setting session that year they racked up 11 Guinness trick-shot records. Today the channel has more than 60 million subscribers, making it one of the biggest sports channels on YouTube, with sold-out arena tours and a headquarters in Frisco, Texas.

sections.h: Every 100,000 views, a kid gets sponsored
sections.p: Dude Perfect's second-ever video, filmed at the Christian summer camp Sky Ranch, came with a pledge: for every 100,000 views, the group would sponsor a child through Compassion International. The video sailed past 18 million views, and the partnership never stopped - Cory Cotton is a longtime child sponsor himself, and the group's 2025 tour offered fans two free tickets for sponsoring a child through Compassion before the show. Trick shots that literally feed kids.

give.text: Sponsor a child through Compassion International, Dude Perfect's longtime partner.

people.label: Mark Rober
people.intro: Mark Rober was born on March 11, 1980, in Orange County, California. This countdown ticks down to the next birthday of the engineer-turned-YouTuber behind some of the internet's biggest science builds.
people.about: A former NASA and Apple engineer, Rober turned elaborate projects, glitter-bomb packages, the world's largest Super Soaker, squirrel obstacle courses, into one of YouTube's most popular science channels. He helped launch the Team Trees and Team Seas fundraisers and founded the build-box company CrunchLabs.

sections.h: The rover engineer with a Halloween side project
sections.p: Rober spent nine years at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, seven of them working on the Curiosity rover now driving around Mars. In October 2011 he strapped two iPads to his chest and back to create the illusion of a see-through torso for Halloween; the video pulled 1.5 million views in a single day. He kept his engineering day job, later designing products at Apple, while the channel grew into one of YouTube's biggest, now past 75 million subscribers.

sections.h: Glitter, fart spray, and engineering justice
sections.p: In December 2018, fed up with porch pirates, Rober built a bait package that blasted thieves with a spinning cloud of glitter and bursts of fart spray while hidden phones filmed their reactions. The video got 25 million views in one day and became an annual holiday tradition. He also holds the Guinness World Record for the largest Super Soaker: seven feet long, pressurized to 2,400 psi, firing water at 272 mph, fast enough to slice a watermelon in half.

sections.h: Ninety million dollars of doing good
sections.p: With MrBeast, Rober co-launched Team Trees in 2019, which raised $20 million to plant 20 million trees with the Arbor Day Foundation, then Team Seas in 2021, which topped $30 million to pull 30 million pounds of trash from oceans and rivers. In 2025 their TeamWater campaign rallied thousands of creators and passed $40 million for clean water with WaterAid, bringing the three drives past $90 million combined. His CrunchLabs build boxes, launched in 2022, get kids engineering at home.

give.text: Give clean water through WaterAid, the partner behind Rober's #TeamWater campaign.

people.label: Gordon Ramsay
people.intro: Gordon Ramsay was born on November 8, 1966, in Johnstone, Scotland. This countdown runs to the next birthday of the Michelin-starred chef and television host.
people.about: Ramsay built a global restaurant empire that has earned multiple Michelin stars, and became a household name through Hell's Kitchen, MasterChef and Kitchen Nightmares. He's also become a social-media force, sharing quick recipes and reaction videos on YouTube and TikTok.

Restaurant Gordon Ramsay in Chelsea has held three Michelin stars since 2001

sections.h: The footballer with the gammy knee
sections.p: Ramsay grew up supporting Rangers and earned a trial with the Glasgow club as a teenager, until a smashed knee cartilage ended the dream. Rather than be known as "the footballer with the gammy knee," he threw himself into cooking at 19, surviving the ferocious kitchens of Marco Pierre White at Harvey's and Albert Roux at Le Gavroche. By 1993 he was head chef at London's Aubergine, earning two Michelin stars in three years before opening his own restaurant in Chelsea in 1998.

sections.h: A quarter century of three stars
sections.p: Restaurant Gordon Ramsay, his flagship in Chelsea, won its third Michelin star in 2001 and has never let go: as of 2026 that is 25 consecutive years at the top, a feat almost no kitchen on earth can match. Across his career Ramsay's restaurants have been awarded 17 Michelin stars in total and currently hold eight. Television turned the perfectionism into a phenomenon, with Hell's Kitchen, Kitchen Nightmares and MasterChef making him the most recognizable chef alive.

sections.h: The soft spot in the world's toughest kitchen
sections.p: With his wife Tana, Ramsay runs the Gordon and Tana Ramsay Foundation, a dedicated fund within Great Ormond Street Hospital Children's Charity in London. The foundation helps seriously ill children get access to pioneering treatments and cutting-edge equipment, and is supporting the hospital's new Children's Cancer Centre. His restaurants invite guests to add a voluntary donation to their bill, and Gordon and Tana raise money personally too, from the Bake It Better baking week to grueling triathlon fundraisers.

give.text: Give to the Gordon and Tana Ramsay Foundation, supporting seriously ill children at Great Ormond Street.

people.intro: Ryan Trahan was born on October 7, 1998, in Eagle Lake, Texas. This countdown ticks down to the next birthday of the YouTuber known for his ambitious challenge series.
people.about: A former competitive runner, Trahan grew a massive YouTube following with viral challenge series, most famously crossing the United States starting with a single penny, and co-founded the candy brand Joyride. He's a frequent MrBeast collaborator.

sections.h: The runner who bet on a water bottle
sections.p: In 2017, Trahan was a freshman cross-country runner at Texas A&M with a small YouTube channel and a water-bottle startup called Neptune Bottle. The NCAA handed him an ultimatum: he could keep competing or keep promoting his company online, but not both. Rather than shut down the business, he walked away from Division I athletics and, eventually, from school itself - betting everything on the channel. The bet paid off spectacularly: that little running vlog grew into one of YouTube's most-watched channels, with more than 20 million subscribers.

sections.h: One penny, thirty days, 196 million views
sections.p: Trahan's signature format sounds impossible on purpose. In June 2022 he started with a single penny in California and spent 30 days flipping it - surveys, lawn mowing, DoorDash runs, reselling water bottles - into enough money to cross the country and hand-deliver the penny to MrBeast in North Carolina. The series pulled in roughly 196 million views in a month and added over two million subscribers. He ran it back in 2023 with an international penny journey, cementing the challenge as a genre of its own.

sections.h: The videos that feed people
sections.p: Trahan turned his stunts into fundraising machines. The 2022 penny series raised $1.38 million for Feeding America - nearly 14 times his $100,000 goal, enough for millions of meals. The 2023 sequel raised about $400,000 for Water.org. Then in 2024 he and his wife Haley visited all 50 states in 50 days, posting a video from each one, and their community raised more than $11.5 million for St. Jude Children's Research Hospital - one of the biggest creator-led fundraisers YouTube has ever seen.

give.text: Fuel childhood-cancer research at St. Jude, the cause of Trahan's 50-state penny run.

sections.h: The loss she kept the tape of
sections.p: In 1993, a preteen Beyonce and her Houston girl group Girl's Tyme flew to Los Angeles for the TV talent show Star Search - and lost to a rock band called Skeleton Crew. She later called it a defining moment of her childhood, and twenty years on she sampled the host announcing the loss in '***Flawless.' The group regrouped as Destiny's Child, and by the late '90s songs like 'Say My Name' had made them one of the best-selling girl groups ever, launching her record-shattering solo career.

sections.h: Thirty-five Grammys and a country crown
sections.p: Beyonce has won 35 Grammy Awards from 99 nominations - more wins than any artist in history. The one that long eluded her, Album of the Year, finally came in February 2025 for Cowboy Carter, the album that had already made her the first Black woman to top Billboard's country albums chart. On the road she is just as unmatched: the Renaissance World Tour grossed $579.8 million in 2023, and the Cowboy Carter Tour added $407.6 million, the biggest country tour ever measured by Billboard.

sections.h: BeyGOOD, from Houston floodwaters to Main Street
sections.p: Beyonce founded BeyGOOD in 2013, and its work is strikingly concrete. When Hurricane Harvey flooded her hometown of Houston in 2017, BeyGOOD partnered with Bread of Life and Texas Southern University to feed and rehouse displaced families. During the pandemic, its Black-Owned Small Business Impact Fund, run with the NAACP, sent $10,000 grants to hundreds of entrepreneurs. Her Homecoming Scholars program has funded students at HBCUs including Xavier, Tuskegee and Morehouse, and the Renaissance tour carried a $2 million commitment to students and small businesses along the route.

people.label: Pope Leo XIV
people.intro: Pope Leo XIV, born Robert Francis Prevost on September 14, 1955, in Chicago, Illinois, is the first American-born pope. This countdown runs to his next birthday.
people.about: An Augustinian friar, Prevost spent much of his ministry as a missionary and later bishop in Peru before being elected pope in May 2025. His papacy made history as the first led by a pope from the United States.
facts: Born September 14, 1955, in Chicago, Illinois
First pope born in the United States, and the 267th pope overall
Elected on May 8, 2025, on the second day of the conclave

sections.h: The White Sox fan who went south
sections.p: Robert Francis Prevost was born in Chicago and grew up in Dolton, just south of the city, earned a mathematics degree from Villanova University in 1977, and joined the Order of St. Augustine. Ordained in 1982, he arrived in Chulucanas, Peru, in 1985 and spent much of the next three decades there as a missionary, seminary teacher and eventually Bishop of Chiclayo, becoming a naturalized Peruvian citizen along the way. He never lost his hometown loyalties: cameras caught the future pope in the stands at Game 1 of the White Sox's 2005 World Series.

sections.h: White smoke and an American first
sections.p: On May 8, 2025, white smoke rose over the Sistine Chapel and Cardinal Prevost stepped onto the balcony of St. Peter's as Pope Leo XIV - the 267th pope and the first ever born in the United States, now leading some 1.4 billion Catholics. His first words to the crowd: 'Peace be with all of you.' He chose the name in tribute to Leo XIII, whose 1891 encyclical Rerum Novarum defended workers in the industrial revolution, saying the church must now answer the new revolution of artificial intelligence.

sections.h: Boots in the floodwater
sections.p: In Peru they called him 'the saint of the north.' When the 2017 El Nino Costero floods destroyed homes across the Chiclayo region, Bishop Prevost didn't just coordinate the church's relief effort - witnesses recall him arriving by truck and loading aid kits himself. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when oxygen was unaffordable for many families, he led the 'Oxygen of Hope' campaign, rallying businesses and citizens to fund two oxygen plants offering free care to the neediest. That hands-on closeness to the poor now shapes his papacy.

give.text: Give to Peter's Pence, the fund Pope Leo XIV uses to reach the poor and disaster-struck worldwide.

sections.h: The Chosen One from Spring Hill
sections.p: By his junior year at Akron's St. Vincent-St. Mary High School, LeBron was such a phenomenon that home games were moved to a university arena and even sold on pay-per-view. In February 2002, Sports Illustrated put the 17-year-old on its cover as 'The Chosen One.' A year later his hometown Cleveland Cavaliers drafted him first overall straight out of high school, and the kid from Akron's Spring Hill apartments began one of the longest primes any athlete has ever had.

sections.h: Passing the record nobody thought would fall
sections.p: On February 7, 2023, a fadeaway jumper against Oklahoma City carried LeBron past Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's 38,387 points, a record that had stood for nearly 39 years. He has since pushed the mark beyond 43,000 and remains the only player with 50,000 combined regular-season and playoff points. Along the way came four championships with three franchises, Miami, Cleveland and the Lakers, and in October 2024 he and his son Bronny became the first father and son to play together in an NBA game.

sections.h: A whole school that keeps its promise
sections.p: The LeBron James Family Foundation does its biggest work blocks from where he grew up. In 2018 it opened the I PROMISE School with Akron Public Schools, and its I PROMISE program now supports well over a thousand Akron students, wrapping in family services and offering graduates free tuition at the University of Akron. Nearby, the foundation converted a landmark ballroom into House Three Thirty, a 60,000-square-foot community hub for job training and financial education.

sections.h: The friendly that changed football
sections.p: In August 2003, an 18-year-old Ronaldo tormented Manchester United's defence in a friendly to open Sporting Lisbon's new stadium. United's players spent the trip home lobbying Sir Alex Ferguson to sign the skinny winger, and within days he was at Old Trafford wearing the famous No. 7 shirt. The boy from Funchal, Madeira, who had left home at 12 to join Sporting's academy, turned that one night into two decades at the very top with United, Real Madrid, Juventus and Al-Nassr.

sections.h: 146 goals for Portugal and counting
sections.p: Ronaldo owns the biggest record in men's international football: 146 goals in 233 appearances for Portugal. At the 2026 World Cup he became the first man to score at six different World Cups, stretching from 2006 to 2026, while pushing his career total past 970 goals for club and country. Add five Ballon d'Or awards, five Champions League titles and the Champions League's all-time scoring record, and the case builds itself, one famously early training session at a time.

sections.h: The quiet donor with no tattoos
sections.p: Ronaldo's giving is unusually personal. A longtime Save the Children ambassador, he keeps his skin tattoo-free so he can donate blood regularly, and he registered as a bone-marrow donor after a teammate's young son was diagnosed with leukemia. He helped fund the Madeira cancer unit that treated his mother, and has repeatedly paid hospital bills for young fans, including funding brain surgery for a 10-month-old boy. Estimates of his lifetime donations run into the tens of millions.

give.text: Give to Save the Children, the charity Ronaldo has championed as its Global Ambassador since 2013.

sections.h: Forty hours of counting
sections.p: Jimmy Donaldson uploaded his first videos as a kid in Greenville, North Carolina, then spent years with friends obsessively studying what made YouTube videos spread. The experiment that finally worked was gloriously absurd: in January 2017 he filmed himself counting to 100,000, a stunt that took more than 40 hours and went viral. From there the formula never changed, just the scale — bigger challenges, bigger giveaways, and production budgets that eventually rivaled television shows.

sections.h: Half a billion subscribers
sections.p: MrBeast passed T-Series in 2024 to become the most-subscribed channel on all of YouTube, and on June 12, 2026, he became the first individual creator in the platform's history to reach 500 million subscribers, livestreaming the moment to hundreds of thousands of viewers. His Amazon competition series Beast Games pushed the giveaways to a new extreme, with 1,000 contestants and the largest cash prize ever awarded on television.

sections.h: A charity built to give everything away
sections.p: Beast Philanthropy is a full YouTube channel whose revenue goes entirely to charity, anchored by a food pantry in eastern North Carolina that distributes more than 100,000 meals a month. With fellow creator Mark Rober he also launched three record-breaking fundraisers: #TeamTrees planted 20 million trees, #TeamSeas pulled 30 million pounds of trash from oceans and rivers, and 2025's #TeamWater raised $40 million for WaterAid — more than $90 million between them.

sections.h: Harvard's first food degree
sections.p: DiGiovanni learned to cook watching his grandmother and great-grandmother in Rhode Island, then talked Harvard into letting him design his own concentration, 'Food and Climate,' the first undergraduate food degree in the university's history. Weeks after graduating in 2019 he appeared on MasterChef season 10, where the 22-year-old became the youngest finalist the show had ever had, finishing third. Instead of the restaurant grind, he bet on short, joyful cooking videos, and tens of millions subscribed.

sections.h: A 46-pound chicken nugget and a bestseller
sections.p: With his beloved collaborator Lynja, DiGiovanni turned record-chasing into a genre: a 97-pound cake pop in 2021, then the world's largest chicken nugget in 2022, a 46.2-pound slab officially certified by Guinness World Records. He has broken multiple food records since. In 2023 he published Knife Drop: Creative Recipes Anyone Can Cook, with a foreword by Gordon Ramsay; it became a New York Times bestseller, complete with QR codes linking recipes to videos.

sections.h: Twenty million pounds of produce
sections.p: DiGiovanni is lead ambassador for The Farmlink Project, a nonprofit that moves surplus produce from farms to food banks instead of landfills. In winter 2022 he fronted a Chipotle campaign built around a 20-million-pound produce-donation goal, with the chain's cult-favorite honey vinaigrette recipe revealed as the reward when donors delivered. He also joined #TeamSeas, the creator-led fundraiser that raised over $30 million to pull 30 million pounds of trash from the world's oceans.

sections.h: From a red wig to a No. 1 debut
sections.p: At 15, Ariana Grande made her Broadway debut in the musical 13 - and then spent four years dyeing her hair cherry red every other week to play Cat Valentine on Nickelodeon's Victorious. In between takes she was quietly building a second life as a singer, posting covers online and recording in whatever hours the set schedule allowed. The bet paid off spectacularly: her 2013 debut album Yours Truly opened at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, and critics immediately compared her whistle-register vocals to Mariah Carey's.

sections.h: Three songs, three top spots
sections.p: On the Billboard Hot 100 chart dated February 23, 2019, Grande held No. 1, No. 2, and No. 3 at the same time - '7 rings', 'break up with your girlfriend, i'm bored', and 'thank u, next' - making her the first act to do it since the Beatles in 1964, and the first solo artist ever. Five years later she conquered a different stage: her turn as Glinda in Wicked, the highest-grossing film adaptation of a Broadway musical, earned her an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress.

sections.h: One Love, and a million hours of therapy
sections.p: Two weeks after the 2017 Manchester Arena attack, Grande returned to the city to headline One Love Manchester before 55,000 people; the broadcast raised over 2.3 million pounds in three hours for the We Love Manchester Emergency Fund, which ultimately raised more than 21 million pounds, and she re-released 'One Last Time' with proceeds going to the fund. She has kept giving since: in 2021 she partnered with BetterHelp to give away free therapy, a program that grew to as much as $5 million in sessions for fans.

sections.h: The contract on a napkin
sections.p: In September 2000, a tiny 13-year-old from Rosario flew to Barcelona for a trial; sporting director Carles Rexach later said he needed less than five minutes to decide. With the deal stalling that December, Rexach grabbed a paper napkin at the Pompeia tennis club and wrote out Barcelona's commitment to sign Lionel Messi - a promise that included paying for the growth-hormone treatment his family could not afford. In 2024 that napkin sold at a Bonhams auction for about $965,000.

sections.h: Eight golden balls and one golden night
sections.p: Messi's numbers read like typos: 672 goals in 778 games for Barcelona, a record 91 goals in the 2012 calendar year, and eight Ballon d'Or awards - more than any player in history. The crowning moment came in Qatar in December 2022, when he scored seven goals, won the tournament's Golden Ball, and lifted the World Cup after a 3-3 final against France decided on penalties - the one trophy that had always escaped him, finally in Argentine hands after 36 years.

sections.h: Health, education, and a place to play
sections.p: Messi created the Leo Messi Foundation in 2007, built around the idea that every child deserves the same shot at their dreams, funding health, education, and sport projects in Argentina and beyond. He has served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador since 2010; in 2019 his foundation gave 200,000 euros to UNICEF projects in Kenya for clean water and food, and, together with the Stavros Niarchos Foundation, it donated the final 2.6 million euros needed to complete funding for the SJD Pediatric Cancer Center in Barcelona, one of Europe's largest.

sections.h: A busted knee and a school musical
sections.p: At Glen Ridge High School in New Jersey, Tom Cruise was a varsity wrestler with hopes of a college scholarship - until a knee injury ended that plan. Recovering and restless, he auditioned for the school production of Guys and Dolls and landed the lead role of Nathan Detroit. That detour became the whole road: he left for New York at 18, took a small part in Endless Love, and by 1983 Risky Business - a $63 million hit - had made the 21-year-old a movie star.

sections.h: The $1.49 billion victory lap
sections.p: Cruise's insistence on doing his own stunts is the stuff of legend: he scaled the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building, for Ghost Protocol and clung to the side of an Airbus A400M during takeoff for Rogue Nation. The payoff came in 2022, when Top Gun: Maverick grossed $1.49 billion worldwide - the first billion-dollar film of his four-decade career - and Cannes surprised him with an honorary Palme d'Or, one of only a handful ever awarded.

sections.h: Quiet checks for Hollywood's own
sections.p: Cruise's most consistent cause is the Motion Picture and Television Fund, the charity that provides healthcare, housing, and services to entertainment-industry workers in need. In 2012 he hosted a charity auction that raised more than $1.2 million for the fund, and he was a key contributor to its $350 million fundraising campaign. He has also lent support to children's health charities, including the Elizabeth Glaser Pediatric AIDS Foundation and the Barbara Davis Center for Childhood Diabetes.

sections.h: The 30-page pitch that changed baseball
sections.p: In the fall of 2012, an 18-year-old Ohtani announced he would skip Japanese pro ball and jump straight to MLB. Every NPB club backed off - except the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters, who drafted him anyway and won him over with a roughly 30-page, data-packed presentation titled 'The Path to Realizing Shohei Ohtani's Dream.' Their bold promise: he could pitch AND hit, something modern baseball had written off. Five seasons later he had a 2016 Japan Series ring, and the two-way experiment was ready for America.

sections.h: The night 50-50 became real
sections.p: On September 19, 2024, in Miami, Ohtani had maybe the greatest single game ever: 6-for-6 with three home runs, two stolen bases, and 10 RBI - becoming the first player in MLB history with 50 homers and 50 steals in a season. He finished at .310 with 54 homers and 59 steals, in year one of a then-record $700 million Dodgers contract. He owns four MVP awards, all unanimous - no other player has even two - plus back-to-back World Series titles in 2024 and 2025.

sections.h: A glove for every school in Japan
sections.p: In November 2023, Ohtani announced he was donating about 60,000 youth baseball gloves - three per school, including left-handed models - to all of Japan's roughly 20,000 elementary schools. 'I'm hoping the kids can spend their days happily with a lot of energy through baseball,' he wrote. It was classic Ohtani: no gala, no naming rights, just gloves showing up at every school in the country so the next kid from a small town like Oshu can start playing catch.

sections.h: The girl in line behind the red bow
sections.p: Gomez's story starts in a casting line: about 1,400 kids showed up to an open call for Barney & Friends, and the girl directly in front of her - wearing a red bow - was Demi Lovato. Both made the seven-kid cut. From there Gomez became a generation's teen idol as Alex Russo on Wizards of Waverly Place (2007-2012), then pulled off the rarest trick in child stardom: growing into an Emmy-nominated adult career, starring in and executive-producing Only Murders in the Building as Mabel Mora.

sections.h: Rare, in every sense
sections.p: In September 2020 Gomez launched Rare Beauty, named after her album Rare, with a mission statement about self-acceptance instead of perfection. It became one of Sephora's best-selling brands, was valued at roughly $2 billion by 2024, and made Bloomberg's headlines that year when it pushed her into billionaire territory. She did it all while being the most-followed woman on Instagram - the first woman ever to pass 400 million followers - and using that megaphone mostly to talk about kindness and mental health.

sections.h: One percent of everything, from day one
sections.p: From the very first product Rare Beauty ever sold, 1 percent of all sales has gone to the Rare Impact Fund, which Gomez created to raise $100 million for youth mental health. It has raised about $30 million so far and supports 30 organizations across five continents - reaching more than 2 million young people a year. Gomez, who has spoken openly about her own mental health, hosts an annual Rare Impact Fund benefit to keep the money and the conversation moving.

sections.h: From Oakland stages to Disney at fourteen
sections.p: Zendaya grew up around the California Shakespeare Theater near Oakland, where her mother worked and she trained as a kid, before starting out as a child model and backup dancer. At 14 she landed Rocky Blue on Disney Channel's Shake It Up, and by K.C. Undercover she had leveraged her star power into a producer credit while still a teenager - shaping the show rather than just starring in it. That instinct to steer her own career is the through-line of everything since.

sections.h: Twenty-four, and the Emmy record fell
sections.p: In 2020, Zendaya won the Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama for playing Rue in Euphoria - at 24, the youngest winner in the category's history. Her second win in 2022 made her the youngest two-time acting Emmy winner ever and the first Black woman to take the category twice. She did it while anchoring giant franchises at the same time: Spider-Man: No Way Home grossed roughly $1.9 billion worldwide, and the Dune films made her half of sci-fi's biggest new saga.

sections.h: Birthdays that feed other kids
sections.p: For her 18th birthday, Zendaya asked fans to skip the presents and fund meals instead, launching a feedONE campaign with Convoy of Hope to feed children in Haiti, Tanzania, and the Philippines - a partnership dating back to her Hurricane Sandy relief work in 2012; she later covered 'All of Me' with proceeds benefiting the organization. Closer to home, her $100,000 gift helped the California Shakespeare Theater - the stage she grew up on - make its post-pandemic summer return.

sections.h: The goalie they called The Wall
sections.p: Before Hollywood, Reeves was a Toronto high-school hockey goalie so hard to score on that teammates nicknamed him 'The Wall.' He broke through as the lovable airhead Ted in Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure (1989), reinvented himself as an action star in Speed (1994), then bet everything on a strange sci-fi script about a hacker who learns reality is a simulation. The Matrix (1999) turned 'whoa' into a career-defining moment and made Neo one of cinema's iconic roles.

sections.h: Three franchises, four decades of hits
sections.p: Few actors have headlined era-defining action movies in the '80s, '90s, 2000s, and 2020s. The Matrix trilogy grossed a combined $1.63 billion worldwide. Then, when many had written him off, a lean 2014 revenge thriller called John Wick grew into a juggernaut: the franchise has now passed $1 billion at the global box office, with Chapter 4 alone earning over $425 million - the series' biggest entry, released when Reeves was 58 years old.

sections.h: The foundation with no name on it
sections.p: After his younger sister Kim was diagnosed with leukemia in 1991, Reeves became her caregiver and quietly funded much of her treatment - she has been in remission for decades. He later created a private foundation supporting children's hospitals and cancer research, telling an interviewer, 'I don't like to attach my name to it, I just let the foundation do what it does.' He has backed Stand Up To Cancer and SickKids, and famously gave Harley-Davidsons to the entire Matrix Reloaded stunt team.

sections.p: Mahomes grew up in big-league clubhouses while his father Pat pitched in MLB, and in 2014 the Detroit Tigers drafted the Whitehouse High righty in the 37th round. He turned them down for Texas Tech, where coach Kliff Kingsbury eventually talked him into going all-in on football. sections.h: Fifty touchdowns, then the trophies
sections.p: In his first season as a starter, Mahomes threw 50 touchdown passes with 5,097 yards and won NFL MVP at age 23. Then came the hardware: Super Bowl titles in the 2019, 2022, and 2023 seasons, with Mahomes named Super Bowl MVP all three times, and the LVII-LVIII repeat was the NFL's first back-to-back championship since the 2003-04 Patriots. His trademark is the impossible comeback -- Kansas City trailed by double digits in each game of the 2019 title run and won anyway.

sections.p: In 2019 Mahomes launched 15 and the Mahomies, a foundation focused on kids' health, wellness, and under-resourced communities. In 2023 he and his wife Brittany committed $1.625 million to Boys & Girls Clubs of America, spread across Greater Kansas City, Lubbock, and his East Texas hometowns of Tyler and Whitehouse -- funding scholarships for up to 300 kids a year. The foundation also pledges $1,500 to the Clubs for every regular-season touchdown he throws, so every score counts twice.

sections.h: The plan written before she was born
sections.p: Richard Williams famously drew up a detailed plan to raise tennis champions before his daughters could hold a racket, then taught Serena and Venus himself on the public courts of Compton. It worked faster than anyone imagined: at the 1999 US Open, a 17-year-old Serena with white beads in her hair beat world No. 1 Martina Hingis in the final, becoming the first Black woman to win a Grand Slam singles title since Althea Gibson in 1958.

sections.h: Twenty-three, one while pregnant
sections.p: Serena's 23 Grand Slam singles titles are the most of the Open Era, alongside four Olympic gold medals and 319 total weeks at world No. 1. The most astonishing of them all came at the 2017 Australian Open, which she won without dropping a set -- beating Venus in the final -- while roughly eight weeks pregnant with her daughter Olympia. She and Venus also went a perfect 14-for-14 in Grand Slam doubles finals together.

sections.h: Schools, healing, and a $111 million fund
sections.p: Through the Serena Williams Fund she has built secondary schools in Kenya and Jamaica, including a 2008 school in Kenya's Makueni County with the Build African Schools initiative, and she serves as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador. With Venus she opened the Yetunde Price Resource Center in Compton, helping families affected by violence in memory of their eldest sister. Her firm Serena Ventures, whose debut fund raised $111 million in 2022, deliberately backs founders who are women or people of color.

people.about: Gates co-founded Microsoft at 19 and helped put a computer on every desk; in his second act, the Gates Foundation became one of the largest private philanthropies in history, focused on global health and education.

sections.h: The demo that had to work the first time
sections.p: In January 1975 Gates was a Harvard sophomore when he and Paul Allen saw the Altair 8800 on the cover of Popular Electronics. They called its maker, MITS, and claimed they had a BASIC interpreter ready to show. They did not — so they wrote one in about eight weeks on a campus mainframe, simulating a chip they had never touched. When Allen typed PRINT 2+2 at the demo in Albuquerque, the machine printed 4. Microsoft was founded that spring.

sections.h: A computer on every desk
sections.p: Microsoft's founding dream — a computer on every desk and in every home — sounded absurd in 1975, when computers filled rooms. Gates drove the company from a two-man shop in Albuquerque to the world's dominant software maker: its 1986 stock offering made him a billionaire at 31, at the time the youngest self-made billionaire ever, and Windows came to run roughly nine out of ten of the world's personal computers. He handed over the CEO job in 2000 to focus on giving the money away.

sections.h: Giving it all away, on a deadline
sections.p: The Gates Foundation gave away more than $100 billion in its first 25 years, much of it to global health: its $750 million pledge helped launch Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, which has since helped vaccinate over a billion children. In May 2025, on the foundation's 25th anniversary, Gates announced it will spend roughly $200 billion more — virtually his entire fortune — and close its doors for good in 2045.

sections.h: Seven decades of preparation
sections.p: Charles became heir apparent at age three, when his mother acceded in 1952, and grew up preparing for a job with no start date. He was the first heir to the British throne to earn a university degree, graduating from Cambridge in 1970, and went on to command the minehunter HMS Bronington in the Royal Navy. In February 1970, aged 21, he gave a speech warning of the threat from plastic waste and pollution — an environmental alarm sounded half a century early.

sections.h: The longest wait for a crown
sections.p: No one in British history waited longer for the throne. Charles was heir apparent for 70 years and Prince of Wales for more than six decades before acceding on September 8, 2022 — at 73, the oldest person ever to become the British monarch. On May 6, 2023, he was crowned alongside Queen Camilla at Westminster Abbey, the first coronation the country had seen in 70 years.

sections.h: A £7,400 bet on young people
sections.p: Leaving the Royal Navy in 1976, Charles used his £7,400 severance pay to fund community projects for struggling young people — the start of The Prince's Trust, now The King's Trust, which has since helped more than a million people aged 11 to 30 with grants, courses and mentoring. One early £1,500 grant sent a teenage Idris Elba to the National Youth Music Theatre; in June 2026 the King knighted him at Windsor Castle.

sections.h: A song for dance class that got away
sections.p: In 2015, Billie's dance teacher asked for a song he could choreograph, so she and her big brother Finneas recorded Ocean Eyes — a track he had written — in his small bedroom studio at their Highland Park, Los Angeles home. They uploaded it to SoundCloud overnight just so he could download it; strangers found it instead, and it racked up hundreds of thousands of plays within weeks. She was 13. Four years later that same bedroom produced a No. 1 debut album.

sections.h: The night she swept the Grammys
sections.p: At the 2020 Grammys, an 18-year-old Eilish became the first artist since Christopher Cross in 1981 — and the youngest ever — to sweep Album, Record and Song of the Year plus Best New Artist in a single night. She and Finneas then won Academy Awards for No Time to Die and Barbie's What Was I Made For?, making her, at 22, the youngest two-time Oscar winner in history and breaking a record that had stood since 1938.

sections.h: Plant-based meals and a cooler planet
sections.p: Eilish's giving runs through Support + Feed, the food-equity nonprofit her mother Maggie Baird founded in 2020, which has delivered more than 2.2 million plant-based meals and pantry items across dozens of cities. Her Overheated climate summits travel with her tours, which favor refillable water stations and plant-based catering. In October 2025 she announced she was donating $11.5 million from her Hit Me Hard and Soft tour to food equity, climate justice and cutting carbon pollution.

sections.h: The kid who wept after Interstellar
sections.p: A LaGuardia High theater kid from Hell's Kitchen, Chalamet landed a role in Christopher Nolan's Interstellar at 18 and assumed it was his big break. At the premiere he discovered how small his part really was - he later admitted he went home and wept for an hour. Three years on came the real break: Luca Guadagnino's Call Me by Your Name, which made him, at 22, the third-youngest Best Actor Oscar nominee ever.

sections.h: From spice deserts to chocolate rivers
sections.p: Few actors have ever stacked hits this fast. Wonka grossed $634 million worldwide in 2023; Dune: Part Two took $715 million in 2024, the year's seventh-biggest film. Then he disappeared into Bob Dylan for A Complete Unknown, spending years learning guitar and harmonica - and at 29 became the youngest Best Actor winner in SAG Awards history. people.label: Martin Luther King Jr.
people.intro: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was born on January 15, 1929, in Atlanta, Georgia. His actual birthday is distinct from the January federal holiday, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, which falls on the third Monday of the month.
people.about: The leader of the American civil rights movement, King preached nonviolent resistance from the Montgomery bus boycott to the March on Washington, where he delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

sections.h: The 26-year-old they turned to
sections.p: King skipped two grades, entered Morehouse College at 15, and took his first pastorate at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery. Barely a year later, after Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in December 1955, local leaders elected the 26-year-old newcomer to lead the boycott - partly because he was new in town and had few enemies. He recalled it happened so quickly he did not even have time to think it through. The boycott lasted 381 days and ended bus segregation.

sections.h: A dream, a quarter-million witnesses
sections.p: On August 28, 1963, King stood at the Lincoln Memorial before some 250,000 people at the March on Washington and delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech, one of the most famous addresses in American history. The next year Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and that October the Nobel Committee named him the Nobel Peace Prize laureate - at 35, the youngest recipient up to that time.

sections.h: The prize money went straight back
sections.p: King gave away his entire Nobel Prize award of $54,123, splitting it among civil rights organizations including the SCLC, CORE, and the NAACP. His legacy is carried on by The King Center in Atlanta, founded by Coretta Scott King in 1968, and by the Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute at Stanford. Since 1994, MLK Day has been a national day of service - Americans honor him each January not with a day off, but a day on.

sections.h: Three encores at thirteen
sections.p: The fourth of twelve children from a one-room cabin on Locust Ridge, Tennessee, Dolly was singing on Knoxville radio at ten. In 1959, introduced by Johnny Cash, the 13-year-old made her Grand Ole Opry debut - and the crowd called her back for three encores. The morning after her 1964 high school graduation she boarded a bus to Nashville, and within a few years The Porter Wagoner Show had made her a country star. Her farewell song to Wagoner became 'I Will Always Love You.'

sections.h: The night she said no to Elvis
sections.p: Elvis Presley wanted to record 'I Will Always Love You,' but Colonel Tom Parker demanded half the publishing rights. Dolly cried all night - then said no, keeping the copyright for her family. Two decades later Whitney Houston's 1992 version became one of the best-selling singles ever, with every songwriting royalty flowing to Dolly. She holds 25 No. 1 Billboard country hits, a record for a female artist, plus 11 Grammy Awards.

sections.h: Books in the mail, checks after the fire
sections.p: Inspired by her father, who never learned to read, Dolly founded the Imagination Library in 1995 to mail free books to children - it passed 200 million books in 2023 and now gifts more than 2 million every month. After the 2016 Gatlinburg wildfires, her My People Fund gave $1,000 a month for six months to every family who lost their home. And her $1 million gift to Vanderbilt in 2020 helped fund Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine research.

sections.h: The demotion that made her
sections.p: Oprah was co-anchoring Nashville's evening news at 19, but in Baltimore the anchor desk didn't fit - WJZ-TV pulled her off the news and parked her on a morning show called People Are Talking. It turned out to be the luckiest demotion in television. In January 1984 she took over Chicago's last-place AM Chicago, and within a month it was the city's top talk show, overtaking Phil Donahue. Two years later it went national as The Oprah Winfrey Show.

sections.h: You get a car! (276 times)
sections.p: The Oprah Winfrey Show ran 25 seasons and 4,561 episodes before ending in 2011, the highest-rated daytime talk show in American television history. On September 13, 2004, she opened a season by giving every audience member a Pontiac G6 - 276 cars in one afternoon, shouting 'You get a car!' twelve times. Her book club turned pick after pick into an instant bestseller, and in 2003 Forbes named her the first Black woman billionaire.

sections.h: A promise kept to Mandela
sections.p: After telling Nelson Mandela she wanted to build a school, Oprah spent $40 million creating the Oprah Winfrey Leadership Academy for Girls, a boarding school for gifted South African girls from disadvantaged backgrounds that opened in 2007. Its first class of 72 graduated in January 2012, every one bound for university. Her Angel Network raised more than $80 million for charities worldwide, and in 2013 President Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

sections.p: Her second-grade choir teacher in Barranquilla turned her away -- the vibrato was too strong, and classmates teased that she sounded like a goat. Shakira kept singing anyway, performed three of her own songs for Sony executives at 13, and walked out with a three-album record deal. After two quiet early releases, 1995's Pies Descalzos made her a Latin American superstar, and she taught herself to write in English for 2001's crossover smash Laundry Service.

sections.h: The anthem the whole planet sang
sections.p: 'Hips Don't Lie' hit No. 1 in 55 countries in 2006, giving Shakira her first Billboard Hot 100 chart-topper. Then 'Waka Waka (This Time for Africa)' became the best-selling World Cup song in history, with more than 10 million copies sold and billions of YouTube views. Add a co-headlining 2020 Super Bowl halftime show, some 95 million records sold, four Grammys and fifteen Latin Grammys, and her global reach speaks for itself.

sections.h: Schools that carry her album's name
sections.p: Shakira named her foundation after the album that made her famous: Fundacion Pies Descalzos, the Barefoot Foundation, founded in 1997 when she was just 20. sections.h: The cut that made him unstoppable
sections.p: As a 5-foot-10 sophomore at Laney High in Wilmington, Jordan was left off the varsity roster -- the coach needed height and kept a 6-foot-7 classmate instead. Stung, Jordan starred on the JV team and practiced in the school gym before class every morning, then grew to 6-foot-3 over the summer and made varsity. By 1982, a freshman at North Carolina, he calmly hit the championship-winning jumper in the NCAA final. The rest is six-ring history.

sections.h: Six rings, never a Game 7
sections.p: Six trips to the NBA Finals with the Bulls, six championships, six Finals MVPs -- and never once did those Finals reach a Game 7. Jordan retired with the highest scoring average in league history at 30.1 points per game, a record 10 scoring titles, five MVP awards and two Olympic golds, including the 1992 Dream Team. The finale was 'The Last Shot': his title-winning jumper over Utah with 5.2 seconds left in Game 6 of the 1998 Finals.

sections.h: The biggest gift in Make-A-Wish history
sections.p: For his 60th birthday in February 2023, Jordan gave Make-A-Wish America $10 million -- the largest donation from an individual in the charity's history, capping more than three decades of personally granting kids' wishes. Closer to home, he has given $17 million to Novant Health to open four Michael Jordan Family Medical Clinics in Charlotte and Wilmington, bringing care to uninsured and underinsured patients in the North Carolina communities where he grew up.

In 2010 he flew to Los Angeles with little more than a guitar, talked his way onto Jamie Foxx's radio show The Foxxhole, and earned a standing ovation within seconds at Foxx's live-music night. Foxx let the unknown teenager sleep on his couch for six weeks and record in his home studio -- and within two years 'The A Team' was a worldwide hit.

sections.p: The Divide tour ran from 2017 to 2019: 255 shows, 8.9 million tickets, and a $776.2 million gross that broke U2's all-time touring record -- often with nothing on stage but Sheeran, a guitar and his loop pedal. 'Shape of You' matched that scale on its own, spending 12 weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100 and becoming the first song ever to reach 3 billion streams on Spotify.

people.about: With The Cat in the Hat, Green Eggs and Ham and How the Grinch Stole Christmas!, Dr. Seuss taught generations to love reading. His books have sold hundreds of millions of copies in dozens of languages.

sections.h: Twenty-seven rejections and one lucky sidewalk
sections.p: Twenty-seven publishers turned down Theodor Geisel's first children's book, And to Think That I Saw It on Mulberry Street. Walking down Madison Avenue with the manuscript, reportedly planning to burn it, he bumped into Dartmouth classmate Mike McClintock, who that very morning had become children's editor at Vanguard Press. McClintock bought the book that day, and Dr. Seuss, a pen name built on his mother's maiden name, was in business.

sections.h: A fifty-word bet he won and never collected
sections.p: In 1957, The Cat in the Hat, written from a strict beginner's vocabulary list, made learning to read feel like mischief. Then publisher Bennett Cerf bet Geisel $50 he couldn't write a book using only fifty different words. The result, Green Eggs and Ham, became one of the best-selling children's books ever, and Cerf famously never paid up. Across more than 60 books, Seuss sold over 600 million copies and earned a special 1984 Pulitzer Prize.

sections.h: The reading party that never ended
sections.p: Geisel died in 1991, but his mission keeps compounding. The Dr. Seuss Foundation, which he incorporated in 1958, still funds early-literacy programs, awarding nearly $900,000 in grants in 2024. His March 2 birthday anchors NEA's Read Across America, the nation's largest celebration of reading with tens of millions of participants. And in his hometown of Springfield, Massachusetts, The Amazing World of Dr. Seuss Museum has welcomed families since 2017.

sections.h: Too small for everyone but Davidson
sections.p: At 6 feet and 160 pounds, Curry got no offers from major programs; even Virginia Tech, where his dad Dell starred, suggested he walk on. So he went to tiny Davidson College, about 1,700 students, and in March 2008 introduced himself to the world: 40 points to stun Gonzaga, then upsets of Georgetown and Wisconsin, averaging 32 points as the Wildcats reached the Elite Eight before falling 59-57 to eventual champion Kansas.

sections.h: The night the record fell at the Garden
sections.p: On December 14, 2021, at Madison Square Garden, Curry passed Ray Allen's 2,973 career three-pointers to become the NBA's all-time leader, needing 511 fewer games (789 to Allen's 1,300). He had already rewritten the season book with 402 threes in 2015-16, the year he became the league's first unanimous MVP. In March 2025 he became the first player ever to reach 4,000 career threes, to go with four championships.

sections.h: Twenty-five million meals in Oakland
sections.p: In 2019, Stephen and Ayesha Curry founded Eat. Learn. Play. to serve the Oakland kids who grew up cheering for him. The foundation has provided more than 25 million meals to Oakland children and families, remodeled 23 schoolyards, redesigned 14 cafeterias, and modernized school libraries across the Oakland Unified School District. In 2023, the Currys committed to raising $50 million more for Oakland's public school students.

She rebuilt herself on the neo-burlesque circuit alongside performance artist Lady Starlight, landed at Interscope in 2007, and impressed Akon so much singing a reference vocal that he pushed to co-sign her. sections.p: In 2012 Gaga and her mother, Cynthia Germanotta, founded the Born This Way Foundation to support young people's mental health. sections.h: Nine, photographed in the school gym
sections.p: When casting scouts swept England looking for Harry Potter's leads, they found Emma Watson through her Oxford theatre teacher and photographed her in her school gym. Eight auditions followed over more than a year, with Watson sitting by the phone at home waiting for each callback - and J.K. Rowling championing her from her very first screen test. Producer David Heyman finally told her she was the 'preferred' candidate, and in 2001 the world met her as Hermione Granger.

sections.h: The 7.7-billion-dollar decade, then Belle
sections.p: The eight Harry Potter films Watson grew up inside grossed over $7.7 billion worldwide, one of the most successful film series ever made. Rather than coast, she enrolled at Brown University mid-franchise and graduated in 2014 with a degree in English literature. Then came her biggest solo swing: playing Belle in Disney's 2017 Beauty and the Beast, which sang its way to about $1.26 billion worldwide and finished as the second-highest-grossing film of that year.

sections.h: Gender equality is your issue too
sections.p: Appointed a UN Women Goodwill Ambassador in July 2014, Watson launched the HeForShe campaign that September with a UN speech inviting men and boys into the fight for gender equality - the first UN campaign of its kind. She has long served as an ambassador for Camfed, which funds girls' education in rural Africa, and founded Our Shared Shelf, a feminist book club that grew into a huge online reading community sharing a new book every couple of months.

sections.h: Seven dollars and a flight home
sections.p: Johnson won a national title with the 1991 Miami Hurricanes, but his NFL dream ended on the Calgary Stampeders' practice roster, earning $300 a week before being cut two months into the 1995 season. Flying home to Miami, he realized he had exactly seven dollars to his name. He turned to the family business - his father Rocky Johnson and grandfather Peter Maivia were both wrestlers - and later named his production company Seven Bucks after that lowest moment.

sections.h: The most electrifying box office in Hollywood
sections.p: As The Rock, Johnson became WWE's first third-generation superstar and a ten-time world champion before pivoting to film - where he became one of the biggest draws alive. Movies with Johnson in a leading role have grossed nearly $11 billion worldwide, with three crossing the billion mark: Furious 7 (over $1.5 billion), The Fate of the Furious, and Moana 2. Forbes crowned him the world's highest-paid actor in both 2019 and 2020.

sections.h: Twenty-one wishes in a single day
sections.p: In December 2023, Johnson pulled off one of the biggest wish days in Make-A-Wish history, granting 21 children's wishes in one day at Universal Studios Hollywood - cooking up his favorite french toast breakfast, then spending five hours with the kids and their families. That same year he and Oprah Winfrey launched the People's Fund of Maui with $5 million each, seeding a relief fund that sent monthly payments directly to roughly 8,100 residents displaced by the wildfires.

sections.p: Adele recorded a three-song demo as a class project at the BRIT School, and a friend posted it to Myspace, where it racked up thousands of plays and caught the ear of XL Recordings. When the indie label called her in, Adele - who only really knew Virgin - assumed they were offering her an office job in A&R. They wanted to sign her instead. She graduated in 2006, signed that year, and released 19 in 2008.

sections.h: The 21 avalanche
sections.p: Her 2011 album 21 became the best-selling album of the 21st century, moving more than 31 million copies and sweeping six Grammys in a single night. The follow-up 25 opened with 3.38 million US copies - the biggest sales week since tracking began in 1991 - while its lead single 'Hello' became the first song ever to sell a million US downloads in one week. Add the Oscar for 'Skyfall' and 16 Grammys, and the numbers speak Tottenham-plainly for themselves.

sections.h: Cake at the fire station
sections.p: Days after the 2017 Grenfell Tower fire, Adele quietly joined mourners at a vigil near the site, then turned up at Chelsea fire station with cake to thank the first responders. She used her Wembley Stadium finale shows that summer to raise money for Grenfell relief, asking every fan to give five pounds. Earlier, on her 21 tour, anyone wanting complimentary or backstage tickets had to donate to Sands, the UK stillbirth and neonatal death charity.

sections.h: Pick number 199
sections.p: Six quarterbacks went ahead of Tom Brady in the 2000 NFL Draft, and his scouting report sneered at his skinny frame and slow feet. When the sixth-rounder met Patriots owner Robert Kraft in the stadium stairwell, he made a promise Kraft never forgot: you'll never regret picking me. A year later an injury to starter Drew Bledsoe put Brady on the field, and he finished that same season lifting the Super Bowl trophy.

sections.h: 28-3, and the greatest comeback ever played
sections.p: Trailing Atlanta 28-3 midway through Super Bowl LI, Brady engineered the biggest comeback in Super Bowl history, winning 34-28 in the game's first-ever overtime. It was ring number five of an eventual seven, the most of any player, six with New England and a seventh with Tampa Bay at age 43. He retired after 23 seasons as the NFL's all-time leader with 89,214 passing yards and 649 touchdown passes, plus five Super Bowl MVP awards.

sections.p: Brady's signature cause is Best Buddies International, the nonprofit building friendships and jobs for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. As a longtime supporter and, since 2019, the organization's global ambassador, he has helped raise more than $46 million through events like the annual Best Buddies Challenge bike ride in Massachusetts. He also launched the TB12 Foundation in 2015 to provide pro bono training and rehab support to young and underserved athletes.

sections.h: The kid who screamed at Robert De Niro
sections.p: Auditioning for This Boy's Life against hundreds of hopefuls, a teenage DiCaprio leapt up mid-scene and screamed "No, it's not empty!" in Robert De Niro's face. De Niro burst out laughing, and DiCaprio walked out certain he had blown it. Instead, De Niro told the filmmakers there was something interesting in that kid, and later tipped off Martin Scorsese. By 19 DiCaprio had an Oscar nomination for What's Eating Gilbert Grape; by 22 he was boarding the Titanic.

sections.h: A billion dollars, then a bear
sections.p: Titanic became the first film in history to gross $1 billion worldwide, holding the all-time box office crown for over a decade and making DiCaprio the most famous actor on Earth. The Oscar itself took longer. It finally came in 2016 for The Revenant, a shoot so brutal he ate raw bison liver and slept inside animal carcasses, and the ovation when his name was read felt like Hollywood exhaling on his behalf.

sections.h: One hundred million dollars for a wilder world
sections.p: DiCaprio started his environmental foundation in 1998, at just 24, and over two decades it granted more than $100 million to over 200 projects across 46 countries, from ocean conservation to indigenous rights. In 2021 that work merged into Re:wild, the conservation group he co-founded, which joined a record $5 billion pledge to protect nature. sections.h: The field trip that changed gymnastics

The coaches were startled enough to send a letter home suggesting lessons. Raised in Spring, Texas by her grandparents Ron and Nellie Biles, who adopted her after her early years in foster care, Simone trained with coach Aimee Boorman from that day on. Ten years after the field trip, at 16, she was all-around champion of the world.

sections.p: The numbers have simply run out of company: 11 Olympic medals, seven of them gold, plus 30 World Championship medals, 23 gold, more than any gymnast in history. At the Paris 2024 Games she came back to win three golds and a silver. And because rules say a skill is named for the first gymnast to land it at a major competition, five skills across vault, beam and floor are officially called 'the Biles.'

sections.h: For the kids who grew up like she did
sections.p: Biles spent part of her childhood in foster care, and she gives back to kids in the same spot. As a national ambassador for Friends of the Children, which pairs vulnerable and foster-care youth with a paid professional mentor for at least 12 years, she helped launch the nonprofit's Houston chapter, put it on a limited-edition Wheaties box, and hosted a Breakfast of Champions celebration in her hometown of Spring, Texas.

give.text: Mentor or fund 12+ years of mentorship for a child through Friends of the Children.

people.label: Bruno Mars
people.intro: Bruno Mars was born on October 8, 1985, in Honolulu, Hawaii. This countdown ticks to the next birthday of pop's ultimate showman.
people.about: A Honolulu kid who impersonated Elvis at four, Mars became modern pop's classic showman: Uptown Funk, 24K Magic, the Silk Sonic project with Anderson .Paak, and a trophy shelf with more than a dozen Grammys on it.
facts: Born October 8, 1985, in Honolulu, Hawaii
Performed as an Elvis impersonator at age 4 in his family's show
'Uptown Funk' topped the Hot 100 for 14 weeks
Has won 16 Grammy Awards
Silk Sonic's 'Leave the Door Open' won Record and Song of the Year (2022)
Performed the Super Bowl halftime show twice

timeline.text: Born Peter Gene Hernandez, October 8, in Honolulu, Hawaii.
Begins performing with his family's band at Waikiki venues, becoming known for a childhood Elvis Presley impersonation act.
Moves to Los Angeles at 17 to pursue music.
Forms the songwriting trio The Smeezingtons, co-writing hits for other artists before his own breakthrough.
Debut album Doo-Wops & Hooligans and "Just the Way You Are" launch his career.
Second album Unorthodox Jukebox released, featuring "Locked Out of Heaven."
Headlines the Super Bowl XLVIII halftime show.
24K Magic released; "Uptown Funk" wins the Grammy for Record of the Year.
24K Magic sweeps 6 Grammys, including Album, Record and Song of the Year.
Forms Silk Sonic with Anderson .Paak, releasing "Leave the Door Open" and the album An Evening with Silk Sonic.
"Leave the Door Open" wins 4 Grammys, including Record and Song of the Year.
"Die With A Smile," with Lady Gaga, reaches No. 1 on the Hot 100.
Releases The Romantic, his first solo album in about a decade, bringing his career total to 16 Grammys.

sections.h: Little Elvis, dropped and undaunted
sections.p: At four years old, Peter Gene Hernandez was performing as a pint-size Elvis impersonator in his family's Honolulu variety show, complete with a cameo in the 1992 film Honeymoon in Vegas. He moved to Los Angeles at 17, signed with Motown, and was dropped within about a year. So he regrouped as a songwriter with his Smeezingtons crew, writing hooks for other artists, until 2010, when 'Just the Way You Are' made Bruno Mars the star he'd been rehearsing to be since preschool.

sections.h: Fourteen weeks of funk
sections.p: 'Uptown Funk,' his 2014 smash with Mark Ronson, sat at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for 14 straight weeks and went on to a Diamond certification. The trophies kept pace: 16 Grammy Awards, including a 2022 night when Silk Sonic's 'Leave the Door Open,' his retro-soul duo with Anderson .Paak, swept both Record and Song of the Year. He headlined the Super Bowl halftime show in 2014 and returned as a guest in 2016.

sections.h: 24K generosity
sections.p: The gold-chains showman gives quietly and locally. In 2017, Mars announced onstage in Michigan that he was donating $1 million from his 24K Magic Tour stop to the Community Foundation of Greater Flint for families hit by the water crisis. The next year he closed the tour at Honolulu's Aloha Stadium and paid for 24,000 Thanksgiving meals for Hawaii residents through the Salvation Army's Hawaiian and Pacific Islands Division, the number a wink at the album.

give.text: Help build Nevada's first standalone children's hospital, the Intermountain Health project Bruno boosted with a $1 million gift.

people.label: Scarlett Johansson
people.intro: Scarlett Johansson was born on November 22, 1984, in New York City. This countdown ticks to the next birthday of Marvel's Black Widow.
people.about: From indie breakthroughs like Lost in Translation to a decade as Black Widow in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Johansson became one of the highest-grossing box-office leads in film history.
facts: Born November 22, 1984, in New York City, three minutes before her twin brother Hunter
The highest-grossing lead actor in film history, at about $14.8 billion
Played Black Widow for over a decade, from Iron Man 2 (2010) to Black Widow (2021)
Earned two Oscar nominations in the same year (2020)
Won a Tony Award for A View from the Bridge (2010)
Released an album of Tom Waits covers, Anywhere I Lay My Head (2008)

timeline.text: Born November 22 in New York City, 3 minutes before twin brother Hunter.
Makes her film debut at 9 in North.
Breaks through in Lost in Translation and Girl with a Pearl Earring.
Releases her debut album, Anywhere I Lay My Head, a collection of Tom Waits covers.
Cast as Black Widow, debuting in Iron Man 2; makes her Broadway debut in A View from the Bridge, winning a Tony.
Earns 2 Oscar nominations in the same ceremony, for Marriage Story and Jojo Rabbit.
Closes out her decade-long MCU run headlining Black Widow.
Becomes the highest-grossing lead actor in film history with Jurassic World Rebirth; makes her directorial debut with Eleanor the Great.

sections.h: Cast without an audition
sections.p: A New York kid who trained at the Lee Strasberg Theatre Institute, Johansson made her film debut at nine in North and earned raves at 13 opposite Robert Redford in The Horse Whisperer. Then came the break every actor dreams about: Sofia Coppola, who had admired her since the indie Manny & Lo, cast the 17-year-old in Lost in Translation without an audition. Her turn opposite Bill Murray in that quiet Tokyo story made her, at 18, a generational star.

sections.h: The $14.8 billion leading lady
sections.p: In July 2025, Jurassic World Rebirth pushed Johansson past Samuel L. Jackson to make her the highest-grossing lead actor in film history, with roughly $14.8 billion across just 36 movies. More than a decade as Black Widow, from Iron Man 2 in 2010 to her own Black Widow in 2021, did the heavy lifting, with hits like Lucy and Sing stacking on top. In 2020 she scored two Oscar nominations in the same year, for Marriage Story and Jojo Rabbit.

sections.h: Keeping the fire stations lit
sections.p: Johansson skipped the 2007 Oscars to tour aid projects in India and Sri Lanka, part of eight years as a global ambassador for Oxfam that also took her to Kenya. Closer to home, she raises money for Solar Responders, the nonprofit founded by her twin brother Hunter after Hurricane Maria, which installs solar panels and battery storage at Puerto Rico's fire stations; its 19 installations have supplied over 1,200 hours of backup power during blackouts.

give.text: Donate to Solar Responders, the family nonprofit Scarlett champions, to keep Puerto Rico's fire stations powered through blackouts.

people.label: Usain Bolt
people.intro: Usain Bolt was born on August 21, 1986, in Sherwood Content, Jamaica. This countdown ticks to the next birthday of the fastest man in history.
people.about: Bolt's 9.58-second 100 m and 19.19-second 200 m world records from 2009 still stand, and his eight Olympic gold medals across three Games made the lightning-bolt pose the most famous celebration in sport.
facts: Born August 21, 1986, in Sherwood Content, Jamaica
100 m world record: 9.58 seconds (Berlin, 2009) - still standing
200 m world record: 19.19 seconds (Berlin, 2009) - still standing
Eight Olympic gold medals across three Games (2008, 2012, 2016)
At 15, became the youngest-ever male world junior champion, winning 200 m gold in Kingston in 2002
His foundation's first project (2010) rebuilt the health centre in his home village

timeline.text: Born August 21 in Sherwood Content, Jamaica.
Wins 200m gold at the World Junior Championships in Kingston at 15, the youngest-ever male world junior champion.
Begins training under coach Glen Mills, a turning point in his career.
Wins 100m, 200m and 4x100m relay gold at the Beijing Olympics, setting world records in all three.
Sets his still-standing world records of 9.58s in the 100m and 19.19s in the 200m at the Berlin World Championships.
Repeats the 100m/200m/4x100m sweep at the London Olympics.
Wins the same triple at the Rio Olympics, completing 3 straight Games sweeps.
Retires at the London World Championships after his final individual race.
Signs a lifetime partnership deal with Puma and releases his debut reggae album, Country Yutes.

records.label: 4x100 m relay world record
records.value: 36.84 seconds, anchoring Jamaica to gold at the 2012 London Olympics — still the standing world record

records.label: Most World Championship gold medals by a male athlete
records.value: 11 golds (2009-2017), a men's record

records.label: Fastest speed ever recorded in a race
records.value: 44.72 km/h (12.42 m/s), reached in the 60-80 m stretch of his 9.58-second 100 m world record run in Berlin, 2009

records.label: Highest annual earnings by a track and field athlete
records.value: $32.5 million (June 2015-June 2016), the majority from endorsements

records.label: Only sprinter to win 100 m and 200 m Olympic titles at three straight Games
records.value: 2008 Beijing, 2012 London and 2016 Rio — a feat no other sprinter has matched

records.label: The stripped relay gold
records.value: Bolt's 2008 Beijing 4x100m relay gold was stripped in 2017 after teammate Nesta Carter's retested sample showed a banned stimulant, undoing what would have been a perfect run of three straight sweeps

sections.h: Shoes on the wrong feet in Kingston
sections.p: Before he was Lightning, Usain Bolt was a cricket-mad kid in rural Trelawny whose fast bowling was so quick that coaches steered him to the track. At 15, he lined up for the 200 m at the 2002 World Junior Championships in front of 36,000 home fans at Kingston's National Stadium - so nervous he put his spikes on the wrong feet. He fixed them, won gold, and became the youngest male world junior champion in history.

sections.h: 9.58 seconds - and a shoelace untied
sections.p: In Beijing in 2008, Bolt won the Olympic 100 m in a world-record 9.69 seconds with one shoelace untied, slapping his chest in celebration 20 metres before the line. A year later in Berlin he ran 9.58 for the 100 m and 19.19 for the 200 m - world records that still stand today. Across Beijing, London and Rio he collected eight Olympic gold medals, and his lightning-bolt pose became the most famous celebration in sport.

sections.h: Giving Sherwood Content a sprinting start
sections.p: Bolt never stopped investing in the tiny village that raised him. The Usain Bolt Foundation's very first project, in 2010, rebuilt Sherwood Content's dilapidated health centre; in 2013 it added a multipurpose sports court with the Digicel Foundation. In 2022 he returned to his old Waldensia Primary school with a free dental outreach mission for students. Under the motto 'Daring Youth to Sprint to Big Dreams', the foundation keeps funding schools and facilities across Jamaica.

give.text: Support the Usain Bolt Foundation's projects for kids in Jamaica.

people.label: Roger Federer
people.intro: Roger Federer was born on August 8, 1981, in Basel, Switzerland. This countdown ticks to the next birthday of tennis's elegant great.
people.about: Federer won 20 Grand Slam singles titles — including a record eight Wimbledons — with a grace that made him the sport's most beloved champion before retiring in 2022 after a 24-year career.
facts: Born August 8, 1981, in Basel, Switzerland
20 Grand Slam singles titles, including a record eight Wimbledons
World No. 1 for 310 weeks - 237 of them consecutive, a record
103 ATP singles titles across a 24-season career
Was a ballboy at the Basel Swiss Indoors in 1993-94, then won the tournament ten times
His foundation has reached about 3 million children through early-education programs

timeline.text: Born August 8 in Basel, Switzerland.
Turns professional and wins the Wimbledon boys' singles title, finishing the year world junior No. 1.
Wins his first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon.
Reaches world No. 1 for the first time, launching a record 237-week consecutive streak.
Loses an epic 5-set Wimbledon final to Rafael Nadal, widely regarded as the greatest tennis match ever played.
Completes the career Grand Slam at the French Open; marries Mirka Vavrinec; twin daughters Myla and Charlene are born.
Twin sons Leo and Lenny are born.
Returns from knee surgery to win the Australian Open, then adds a record 8th Wimbledon title.
Loses an epic Wimbledon final to Novak Djokovic despite holding 2 championship points, the longest final in Wimbledon history.
Announces his retirement and plays his farewell match alongside Rafael Nadal at the Laver Cup.

records.label: Consecutive Grand Slam semifinals
records.value: 23 in a row, 2004 Wimbledon to the 2010 Australian Open — the men's record, well clear of the previous mark of 10 shared by Rod Laver and Ivan Lendl

records.label: Consecutive Grand Slam finals
records.value: 10 straight major finals during his mid-2000s peak, an Open Era men's record

records.label: Longest grass-court win streak
records.value: 65 consecutive match wins on grass, 2003-2008 (10 straight titles, five at Wimbledon and five at Halle) — the longest tour-level grass-court streak of the Open Era, ended by Rafael Nadal in the 2008 Wimbledon final

records.label: Wimbledon match wins
records.value: 105 career match wins at the All England Club stood as the men's record for years — surpassed by Novak Djokovic, who reached 106 wins in July 2026

records.label: Career prize money
records.value: $130,594,339 in on-court prize money — trailing only Novak Djokovic and Rafael Nadal on the all-time list

records.label: Highest-paid athlete in the world (2020)
records.value: Topped Forbes' global athlete earnings list with $106.3 million for 2020 — about $100 million of it from endorsements — becoming the first tennis player ever to lead the ranking

sections.h: The ballboy who beat the king
sections.p: Federer's tennis life began as a ballboy at his hometown Swiss Indoors in Basel in 1993-94 - a tournament he would later win ten times. The world took notice on July 2, 2001, when the 19-year-old with the ponytail stunned seven-time champion Pete Sampras in five sets at Wimbledon, snapping Sampras's 31-match win streak there. Two years later Federer lifted his first Wimbledon trophy, and an era began.

sections.h: 237 weeks without letting go
sections.p: The numbers still read like typos: 20 Grand Slam singles titles, including a record eight Wimbledons; 103 ATP titles; and 310 total weeks at world No. 1 - 237 of them consecutive, a streak from 2004 to 2008 that no player has come close to matching. He said goodbye in September 2022 at the Laver Cup, playing his final match alongside his greatest rival, Rafael Nadal, after 24 professional seasons.

sections.h: Preschools from Basel to Malawi
sections.p: Federer started the Roger Federer Foundation in 2003, the same year he won his first Grand Slam title, focusing on early-childhood education in Lesotho, Malawi, Namibia, South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe and Switzerland. By the end of 2024 it had reached roughly 3.1 million children and supported more than 59,000 teachers, investing over $50 million in thousands of kindergartens and elementary schools so kids arrive at first grade ready to learn.

give.text: Fund early-childhood education across southern Africa through the Roger Federer Foundation.
